---
title: staleTimes
description: Learn how to override the invalidation time of the client cache.
version: experimental
---

`staleTimes` is an experimental feature that enables caching of page segments in the [Client Cache](/docs/app/glossary#client-cache).

You can enable this experimental feature and provide custom revalidation times by setting the experimental `staleTimes` flag:

```js filename="next.config.js"
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    staleTimes: {
      dynamic: 30,
      static: 180,
    },
  },
}

module.exports = nextConfig
```

The `static` and `dynamic` properties correspond with the time period (in seconds) based on different types of [link prefetching](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch).

- The `dynamic` property is used when the page is neither statically generated nor fully prefetched (e.g. with `prefetch={true}`).
  - Default: 0 seconds (not cached)
- The `static` property is used for statically generated pages, or when the `prefetch` prop on `Link` is set to `true`, or when calling [`router.prefetch`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router).
  - Default: 5 minutes

> **Good to know:**
>
> - [Loading boundaries](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) are considered reusable for the `static` period defined in this configuration.
> - This doesn't affect [partial rendering](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#client-side-transitions), **meaning shared layouts won't automatically be refetched on every navigation, only the page segment that changes.**
> - This doesn't change [back/forward caching](/docs/app/glossary#client-cache) behavior to prevent layout shift and to prevent losing the browser scroll position.

### Version History

| Version   | Changes                                                    |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `v15.0.0` | The `dynamic` `staleTimes` default changed from 30s to 0s. |
| `v14.2.0` | Experimental `staleTimes` introduced.                      |

---
title: staleTimes
description: Learn how to override the invalidation time of the client cache.
version: experimental
---

`staleTimes` is an experimental feature that enables caching of page segments in the [Client Cache](/docs/app/glossary#client-cache).

You can enable this experimental feature and provide custom revalidation times by setting the experimental `staleTimes` flag:

```js filename="next.config.js"
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    staleTimes: {
      dynamic: 30,
      static: 180,
    },
  },
}

module.exports = nextConfig
```

The `static` and `dynamic` properties correspond with the time period (in seconds) based on different types of [link prefetching](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#prefetch).

- The `dynamic` property is used when the page is neither statically generated nor fully prefetched (e.g. with `prefetch={true}`).

- The `static` property is used for statically generated pages, or when the `prefetch` prop on `Link` is set to `true`, or when calling [`router.prefetch`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router).
  - Default: 5 minutes

> **Good to know:**
>
> - [Loading boundaries](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) are considered reusable for the `static` period defined in this configuration.
> - This doesn't affect [partial rendering](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#client-side-transitions), **meaning shared layouts won't automatically be refetched on every navigation, only the page segment that changes.**
> - This doesn't change [back/forward caching](/docs/app/glossary#client-cache) behavior to prevent layout shift and to prevent losing the browser scroll position.

Back navigation is fast thanks to bfcache via the router, 10-47ms. Local numbers look fine since the DB is remote Supabase with some latency, but the real slowness users feel is likely on the dev server where compilation dominates, or on the deployed Vercel instance — the cold home load at 2.4s stands out as the biggest issue.

But the bigger clue is navFeedback: for organization/investigations/spending/agents it's 150-600ms, meaning clicks produce no visible response for half a second — that's the "laggy" feel. Rail items like accounts/plan/wealth show ~50ms feedback because their loading boundary appears instantly, while the slow ones seem to use IntentLink with full prefetch={true}, so the click waits on an in-flight full page prefetch instead of immediately showing the loading state.

The notifications nav is also huge at 1386ms, and home's 2.4s cold load is clearly the biggest problem since "settled" requires every Suspense boundary to resolve. I also need to factor in the user's complaint about chat response time and artifact rendering speed. Rather than trying to measure server promise timing directly, I think the practical approach is to watch the browser timeline on a cold Home load and record exactly when each "Loading…" fallback disappears, to pinpoint which section is the real bottleneck.

content.thinking: I'm wondering if the HTML shell timing versus body completion is getting confused by streaming suspense boundaries, so I want to verify with actual browser performance timing instead of guessing — maybe my evaluation failed because the main element doesn't exist yet when I query for it.

The h1 timing is odd — the document finishes streaming at 960ms but the h1 doesn't actually appear until 1451ms, which suggests the page is waiting on that big Promise.all before rendering anything, even though loading.tsx should show a skeleton in the meantime. I'm puzzled since the h1 should be server-rendered, not dependent on hydration.

The real culprit is Home blocking on the ~900ms Promise.all for net worth, projections, and goals data. A better approach is splitting the header/shell from the data-dependent grid, using Suspense boundaries around each widget so net worth, upcoming projections, and goals each stream independently as their own data resolves, while the fast layout data renders immediately. Before refactoring, I want to measure where the 900ms actually goes by adding temporary timing instrumentation, though rebuilds are slow so I'm considering using the dev server instead for faster profiling iterations.

A standalone timing script would need auth/cookies, so a service-role client bypassing RLS could work, but path aliases and "server-only" imports complicate running outside Next's build. I'll just spin up a dev server on port 3001 alongside the prod build — since Next 16 separates dev output into `.next/dev`, there's no conflict — and add temporary timers around each promise in Home's Promise.all to see which one is slow.

I'm also considering whether server actions already call `revalidatePath`, which would mean bumping `staleTimes.dynamic` to something like 30-60s could make revisits instant without sacrificing freshness. The real bottleneck seems to be pure data latency on Home (~800ms), compounded by full re-renders on each visit. I'm also suspecting the nav feedback delay on tab links comes from IntentLink's hover-triggered full prefetch — clicking mid-prefetch might force the router to wait for completion instead of showing loading.tsx immediately, which would explain inconsistent delays between rail items and other nav links.

I'm also noting that CDN script loads (chart.js etc.) get browser-cached across sandboxed iframe loads despite opaque origins.
